card.title: The definite integral as an area under a curve

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The **definite integral** converts area into analysis: partition, erect rectangles, sum — and the **Riemann sum** Σf(xᵢ*)Δxᵢ, refined without end, *defines* ∫ₐᵇ f dx. The integral measures **signed** area (above +, below −): ∫₀^π sin x = 2 (the hump), while the full period gives 0 (cancelling lobes).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - ∫ₐᵇ f dx = lim_{n→∞} Σ f(xᵢ*)Δxᵢ = F(b) − F(a) - additivity: ∫ₐᵇ + ∫ᵦᶜ = ∫ₐᶜ; reversal: ∫ᵇₐ = −∫ₐᵇ - ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3; ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: x Definite integral always positive. x Can be negative if curve is below x-axis.  ·  x int f(x)dx = F(x) + C (definite). x C cancels in definite integrals.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: A definite integral can be negative, because the region below the x-axis contributes negatively; only the area given by int |f(x)|dx is never negative.  ·  The power rule for integration fails at n = -1, so int 1/x dx = ln|x| + C keeps the absolute value bars, and the integrand is undefined at x = 0.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The cancelling lobes*** - sine over a full period integrates to 0: the hump above the axis and the trough below cancel - signed area in action.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: x Area = int f(x)dx always. x Use |f(x)| for total geometric area.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Evaluate a definite integral by finding an antiderivative F and computing F(b) - F(a) at the two limits.  ·  Find the area under a curve from a to b, deciding from the sign of f whether the answer is the integral itself or the integral of |f(x)|.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Anti-derivative, then F(b) - F(a). No +C. Watch limit order (reversal flips sign). Signed area: negative integrands subtract.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2022 (verified PYQ): Evaluate ∫₀¹ x² dx. (2m)** — **Anti-derivative:** F(x) = x³/3 (power rule reversed). **FTC Part 2 (evaluation theorem):** ∫₀¹ x²dx = [x³/3]₀¹ = F(1) − F(0) = **1/3 − 0 = 1/3**. **No +C:** any constant in F cancels in the subtraction — definite integrals are numbers, not families.…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): Compute ∫₀^π sin x dx and interpret the result as signed area.** — **Anti-derivative:** ∫sin x dx = −cos x. **Evaluate:** ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = (−(−1)) − (−1) = 1 + 1 = **2**.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Write the bracket evaluation [F(x)] with limits shown - the substitution display is the expected working for FTC Part 2.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The FTC is the dictionary between the two halves of calculus: accumulation functions differentiate back (Part 1) and evaluation needs only one anti-derivative (Part 2).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Definite integral: Riemann sum Sigma f(x_i*) Delta x_i refined to the limit - area under y = f(x) from a to b, signed (above +, below -). Properties: linearity, additivity (a to b plus b to c = a to c), reversal (integral b a = - integral a b), zero width, domination, m(b-a) <= integral <= M(b-a).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Odometer trip distance is a definite integral of speed from start to finish time - F(b) - F(a) with the starting point as the lower limit.

Sum = Σᵢ f(xᵢ)Δx = Σ (3i/n)²·(3/n) = (27/n³)Σi².…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Area Becomes a Limit **The definite integral as area under a curve**: Riemann sums, the limit definition, and the Fundamental Theorem that makes evaluation algebraic.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The area problem - Area under y = f(x) ≥ 0 from a to b: partition [a, b] into n subintervals, erect rectangles of height f(xᵢ*), sum the areas — the **Riemann sum** Σf(xᵢ*)Δxᵢ. Refine: **∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = lim_{n→∞} Σ f(xᵢ*)Δx** — the definite integral. - **Notation:** ∫ (elongated S for sum), a and b the limits, dx the width differential.…  ·  ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Riemann sum** | Rectangle-area total | Σf(xᵢ*)Δx | | **Definite integral** | Limit of Riemann sums | ∫ₐᵇ f dx | | **Signed area** | Above +, below − | sine over a period = 0 | | **FTC Part 2** | F(b) − F(a) | evaluation bridge |

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: An antiderivative of a continuous f exists on [a, b] and the definite integral exists there too, so F(b) - F(a) is always well defined.  ·  int_a^b f(x)dx depends on the limits as well as on f, so two different integrals of the same function can differ in value and even in sign.  ·  Adding a constant to f changes the integral by that constant times (b - a), not by the constant itself.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why the limit definition matters - The Riemann limit is the *definition* — it makes "area under a curve" precise for curved boundaries where geometry fails, and it is the license for every property (linearity, additivity) proved from sums.…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables **Indefinite vs definite** | Feature | Indefinite ∫f dx | Definite ∫ₐᵇ f dx | |---|---|---| | Output | family F + C | number | | Meaning | anti-derivative | signed area | | Constant | required | cancels | | Tool | table/rules | FTC Part 2 |  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **No +C in definite integrals:** the evaluation theorem subtracts — constants cancel by construction. **Negative integrals are fine:** f < 0 gives ∫ < 0 — signed area; geometric area needs ∫|f|. **Limits order:** ∫ᵇₐ = −∫ₐᵇ — flipping the limits flips the sign.
